title: Live Wire
summary: Push a goal to 50,000 phones within a second: polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets — and how to scale open connections.

goals.text: See why plain HTTP can't push and what polling costs
Compare long polling, SSE and WebSockets
Fan out across connection servers with pub/sub
Track presence with heartbeats and TTLs
Survive deploys without a reconnect storm

steps.title: A goal nobody hears about
body: Pitchside shows live scores for amateur football leagues. A volunteer scorer taps “Goal!” on a laptop by the pitch; the event lands in the Match API.
But HTTP only answers questions. Until a fan's phone asks again, the server has no way to tell it anything — the goal sits in the database while fans stare at 1–1.

card.title: HTTP speaks when spoken to
lines: server has news → no way to say it
! fans see the goal only on refresh

steps.title: Are we there yet?
body: The simplest fix is short polling: every phone asks “anything new?” every 2 seconds. It works through every firewall and proxy, and a fan sees a goal at most 2 seconds late.
Almost every answer, though, is “no”.

card.title: Short polling
lines: news appears ≤ 2 s late, ~1 s on average

steps.title: Paying for silence
body: Cup final day: 50,000 fans. At 30 polls a minute each, that's 25,000 requests per second — and about 97% of them come back empty. The API fleet is sized for questions with no news.
Poll faster for fresher scores and the cost rises; poll slower and fans hear the crowd cheer before their phone does. Polling makes you trade freshness against load.

steps.title: Ask once, wait for news
body: With long polling the server doesn't answer “nothing yet”; it holds the request open until something happens or ~30 s pass. The fan gets the goal almost instantly, then immediately asks again.
Requests drop from 30 to about 2 per fan per minute. The cost moves elsewhere: 50,000 requests are now open at once, so the server must hold many idle connections cheaply.

card.title: Long polling
lines: client asks; server holds the request

steps.title: One response that never ends
body: Server-Sent Events make the long wait official: the phone opens one HTTP request and the server streams events down it as they happen. It's plain HTTP, the browser reconnects automatically, and the Last-Event-ID header lets it resume without gaps.
SSE is one-way — perfect for scores, notifications and feeds, where the client mostly listens.
changes: + Event stream from server to fans

card.title: Server-Sent Events
lines: one GET, the response never ends

steps.title: Both sides talk
body: Pitchside adds match chat. Now fans send too, many times a minute. A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with an Upgrade header and becomes a persistent two-way channel: small messages flow both ways with no per-message HTTP overhead.
Use it when the client talks as much as it listens — chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing.

callout.text: If you only push one way, SSE is simpler: it works with ordinary HTTP tooling and reconnects for free.

card.title: WebSockets
lines: # needs LB + proxies that allow long upgrades

steps.title: Your friends are on another server
body: One server can't hold 50,000 busy sockets with room to spare, so Pitchside runs three connection servers. Each socket is pinned to the server it connected to.
A fan on #1 posts “What a goal!”. Server #1 pushes it to its own 16,000 sockets — and the 34,000 fans on #2 and #3 see nothing.
changes: ~ Each fan pinned to one server

card.title: 12,000 sockets per server
lines: each fan is pinned to one socket server
#1 can only push to its own sockets
! fans on #2 and #3 never see it

steps.title: Publish once, every server delivers
body: Connect the servers with a pub/sub backplane (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS or a message broker). Each socket server subscribes to channels for the matches its fans are watching.
A message arriving at any server is published once to match:812; every subscribed server receives it and pushes it down its own sockets. Servers stay stateless towards each other.
changes: ~ Messages reach fans on every server

card.title: A shared backplane
lines: bus fans it out to all subscribers
= each server pushes to its own fans

steps.title: Who's watching right now?
body: Presence (“48,210 watching”) can't rely on clean disconnects — phones drop into tunnels without saying goodbye. Instead, clients send a heartbeat every 30 s and the server refreshes a key with a TTL in a shared store.
Miss two heartbeats and the key expires: that fan is offline. Counts are approximate by design, and that's fine for a badge.

card.title: Who's here?
lines: # count online per match, not per server

steps.title: Long-lived connections, short-lived servers
body: Restarting server #2 cuts 16,000 sockets. If all clients reconnect instantly, the survivors take a reconnect storm on top of normal traffic.
Clients should wait a random delay (jitter) and back off on failure; servers should drain: stop accepting new sockets, then close existing ones gradually.

Short pollingrare updates, simplest setup
Long pollingfallback where streams are blocked
SSEserver → client feeds
WebSockettwo-way, chatty clients

card.title: 16,000 reconnects
lines: # drain: stop new sockets, then close slowly

steps.title: Keep the line open
body:
• Polling trades freshness for load; most answers are empty.
  • Long polling holds requests open until there's news.
  • SSE streams server → client over plain HTTP; WebSockets go both ways.
  • Open connections pin users to servers — fan out through a pub/sub backplane.
  • Presence = heartbeats + expiring keys.
  • Reconnect with jitter and drain servers before deploys.
